newsitem.title: FRANCE: French police fail to link gunpowder users to bomb.
newsitem.headline: French police fail to link gunpowder users to bomb.

text.p: French police raided the homes of 163 people on Tuesday known to have bought gunpowder but could not link any of them to a crude bomb that killed four people in a train in central Paris last December.

About 500 police, helped by French intelligence services, took part in the swoops in Paris and the surrounding region starting before dawn. The 163 people were quizzed at their homes but no one was remanded in custody.
Police said most were legal hunters, sharpshooters or gun collectors. One woman said she bought the explosive for use in a ritual to break a spell cast by a Moslem priest.
"We're leaving nothing to chance. All the investigations are being done and well done by the scientific and technical police," said Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre.

"We have systematically obtained fingerprints in the Metro underground, from the bomb, and investigations are under way and I can tell you they will be completed more quickly than you think," he told Europe 1 radio. He gave no details.
One police officer said the gunpowder checks were "a very large operation that closes a door" of the inquiry. He said they were "negative overall".

Police suspect that Algerian Moslem militants, battling Algiers' military government, planted the bomb that exploded aboard a train in the Port Royal station during the afternoon rush hour, killing four and injuring 90.

The people questioned on Tuesday had all bought gunpowder matching the explosive used in the crude bomb, between July and December. Anyone buying gunpowder in France has to present an identity card and their name is registered with the purchase.
Police had tracked down purchase slips for 123 kg (360 lbs).

France sharply stepped up security following the blast, assigning soldiers armed with automatic weapons to patrol train stations, airports and popular tourist sites and sealing off public rubbish bins in Paris.
Police have also staged several raids of suspected Moslem militants but have made no arrests and apparently have little to go on so far in the probe.

Algerian Moslem militants claimed responsibility for a series of bombings that struck France in 1995, killing eight people and injuring 200. They accuse Paris of backing the military government in a bloody conflict against them.

About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which the Islamic Salvation Front, later banned, had taken a huge lead.
